subject: dutchWindmill
pitch:
Category: Architecture.
Subject: Dutch windmill.
Style: Animal Crossing.

spec.name: Dutch Windmill (Animal Crossing)
spec.description: A chubby, cozy Animal Crossing style Dutch windmill with a stone base, tapered thatched-brick tower, rotating cap and four lattice sails, on its own small footprint.
spec.layout: Squat, rounded octagonal tower tapering upward, centred on x=0, facing +Z. A wide stone plinth sits on the floor, then a cream plastered brick body with a red-brown trim band, a front door with a little step, round-top windows and a balcony (gallery) ring partway up. A domed red-roofed cap sits on top with a small tail pole and ladder at the back, and a hub on the front (+Z) of the cap carries four big wooden lattice sails in an X shape, tilted slightly toward the viewer. Everything is chunky and soft with bevelled, faceted primitives; flat pastel colours, warm tops and cooler undersides, little props like flower boxes, a lantern and a sack of flour at the door.

parts.builds: Stone plinth (octagonal, two stacked tiers in stone/stoneDark with stone block seams as small parts), small grass tuft ring hugging the plinth, flagstone path stub to the door, and the door step. Keep simple, sized to the footprint.
parts.attaches: Top at plinthTop; tower stands on towerBase; path ends at doorFront.

parts.builds: Tapered octagonal tower from radius ~1.55 at the base to ~1.05 at the top in wall cream, with a brick-coloured lower skirt band, trimWood bands at bottom, mid and top, vertical corner ribs in wallShade, small brick patches, and a rounded top ring. Includes the gallery balcony ring at galleryDeck (wood deck, posts, rail).
parts.attaches: Stands on towerBase; cap sits on towerTop; door and windows are mounted on its surface by the detail part.

parts.builds: Front door in teal with a round top, frame, planks, golden knob and hinges, a lantern beside it glowing, a sack of flour and barrel by the door. Round-top windows (windowFrame surround, window glass, shutters in teal, cross bars) at three heights around the tower, flower boxes with pink and yellow flowers and leaves under the front windows, and a small loft hatch.
parts.attaches: Seated on the tower surface at doorFront and around the tower; rides base joint.

parts.builds: Domed cap on capCentre: a roof lathe in roof red with lighter shingle rows as small parts, a trim ring at the eaves, a tiny finial with a golden ball on top, a small round gable window, the front axle housing and hub boss at hubFront, and at the back a tail pole with a ladder (wood rails and rungs) running down toward the ground.
parts.attaches: Sits on towerTop; hub at hubFront connects to the sails joint; tail pole ends at tailPoleBack.

parts.builds: Four big lattice sails of sailFrame wood crossing at a spinning hub at hubFront: each has a long main spar, a thinner outer rail, many cross-bars and cream sailCloth panels on the leading half in alternating neat patches, a rounded tip cap, and small colour pennant ribbons on the tips (roof and flowerYellow). A hub cap in darkWood with golden nail studs. Arms extend ~2.2 m from the hub, tilted slightly outward, one pair vertical and one horizontal in rest pose (plus-shape rotated 45 degrees to an X), all rigid on the sails joint.
parts.attaches: Centred on mount hubFront, riding the sails joint.

I'm sketching out the buildBaseAndGround function, planning to keep it fairly compact using the shared geometry helpers, and roughing out the footprint dimensions for the base.

Still working out the octagonal plinth geometry...

Confirming that rotating the cylinder by 22.5° about Y aligns faces at the 0° position, and working out door placement details—the door sits near the apothem radius around z 1.45, with the plinth tiers extending further out to z 1.66 and 1.85, and a step box reaching toward z 2.4 for the path.

Still working out the staircase steps...

Still working out the step heights and z-ranges...

I'm shortening the stairs to fit within the box, placing step one near z 1.85–2.1, then laying flagstone path stones just after it with a scattered row spanning the width to fill out the remaining depth.

Now I'm plotting a curved path of about seven flattened octagonal flagstones bending toward +x as they approach z 2.4, sized small enough to stay within the box bounds, and setting their height so the bottoms sit flush with the floor at y=0.

Next I'm placing a ring of grass tufts around the plinth's lower tier, skipping the front door/path region, and computing each tuft's radial offset based on the octagon's boundary distance at its angle so they hug the shape naturally while staying clamped inside the box.

Given my part budget, I'm cutting down the tuft count from 28 to 20 and simplifying each tuft to just two cones (one tall, one short and leaning) instead of three, keeping the total part cost manageable, and considering adding a handful of tiny white flowers scattered through the grass for extra detail.

Now I'm working out the tower's tier structure: a cooler stoneDark lower tier, a lighter stone upper tier, and a thin stoneLight cap ring at the very top, pinning down exact heights and radii for each layer so they stack cleanly without gaps.

For the upper tier, I'm thinking simpler geometry: use a thin ring cylinder per tier for horizontal seams, then just vertical seam boxes per face—16 for the upper tier versus 24 for the lower, keeping it light on part count.

Working out seam block colors and dimensions now, using a darker stone tone for the lower tier and a lighter one above, with each seam positioned flush against the face surface using tangent-direction math to compute position and orientation per angle.

I'll add small decorative touches too: patches of moss on upward-facing surfaces near the bottom, a dirt ring around the base footprint, and grass tufts just outside that, plus confirming the joint hierarchy attaches correctly to the base for rotation.

For the steps, I'll give each one a lighter stone cap slab on top for contrast, then scatter a few pebbles and small flower tufts (tiny colored spheres on stems) near the landing for extra life.

I'm keeping the palette tight — using leaf and grass greens plus six new tones for stone, seam, dirt, two flag colors, and dark grass. Now I'm figuring out moss patches along the narrow ledge between the lower and upper tiers, sizing them to fit that thin 0.19-wide strip near the corners.

Working out the tilt and yaw for the cone tufts, realizing default Euler rotation order won't give the outward lean I want, so I'll need a different rotation order or build a quaternion directly.

Checking that the tilted cone's base stays close enough to ground level within the 2% tolerance, then moving to the octagon face-angle logic: computing each face's angular offset from its nearest 45° center to determine distance falloff per facet.

For the tufts, I'm planning around 24 clusters spaced around the circle, skipping a front wedge near 0° for the path stones, each cluster getting a tall main blade and a shorter offset side blade with randomized variation, plus a handful of small flower spheres placed near select tufts.

Now I'm tallying up the total element count across tiers, seams, steps, flagstones, tufts, flowers, moss, and pebbles — it's coming out slightly over budget, so I'm trimming by reducing seam density per face and cutting back the flower count to keep the total manageable.

Placing flagstones along a curving path with varying sizes, keeping z-scale modest. Now I'm thinking through the code structure—minimal triangles, reusing palette keys like stone, leaf, and flower colors, and deciding which mounts actually get used.

I'm building a placement helper that rotates octagonal cylinder segments by yaw and tilt angles, reusing the door-front reference for consistent z-alignment and seam placement around the ring.

I'm setting up the buildSails function signature using the provided context type, then starting to define the hub position at the front of the structure.

For the sails, I'm figuring out the arm box dimensions (extending outward from the hub with a slight forward tilt), and designing a helper function that maps arm-local coordinates into world space by computing a direction vector per arm angle, then applying a Z-axis rotation plus a small tilt rotation so each arm's geometry sits correctly in 3D.

Writing the quaternion math...

I'm working out the hub cap geometry, placing a darkWood cylinder with studs in front of the hub, and adjusting arm tilt and depth so the arms sit behind the hub boss without clipping through it, landing on a 6° tilt with the spar depth around 0.08-0.1.

Then I shift to the rest pose orientation of the arms, trying to reconcile whether it's an X-shape at 45°/135°/225°/315° or a plus-shape with one vertical and one horizontal pair—the bounding box dimensions suggest the plus arrangement, so I'm reworking the angles and tip positions accordingly.

Checking clearance against the gallery rail, I realize the plus shape's bottom arm would collide with the deck railing, while the X shape clears it better since its tips sit higher up. I'll go with the X shape and extend the arm length to about 2.2m to better fill the available box.

Now I'm laying out each sail's internal structure: a main spar running along the center of the arm, with a thinner trailing rail offset to one side forming the lattice framework typical of real windmill sails.

Laying out the lattice sail geometry: outer rail and end bars as boxes, nine evenly spaced cross-bars along the frame, plus a couple of longitudinal lattice bars, with cloth panels filling the gaps in an alternating pattern.

I'll also add a trailing-side element: a small windboard made of five spaced slat boxes on the trailing edge, using a lighter frame color, to break up the leading-half cloth pattern.

Then I'm capping the arm tips with rounded spheres for the end caps and corner knobs, plus adding colorful swallowtail pennant ribbons flowing outward beyond each tip, alternating roof-color and yellow across the four arms.

Still defining pennant shape...

Checking the ribbon extension against the box bounds confirms everything stays within limits even at the 45° arm angles. Now I'm designing the hub itself: a dark wood boss cylinder with a domed front, plus a ring of eight golden nail studs arranged around the hub face.

Still refining hub geometry...

Cloth fills the bays between bars with a slight inset gap, and I'm deciding on colors now — sail frame and dark wood from the palette, plus a lighter wood tone and a subtle cloth tint variation for visual texture.

I'm now tallying the part counts per arm: one spar, outer rail, inner bar, tip bar, nine crossbars, one longitudinal piece, eight cloth cells across the bays, five windboards, a tip cap sphere, and corner knobs.

Adding the pole, ribbons, knot, and gold studs brings each arm to roughly 36 pieces, so four arms total around 144. The hub adds a boss, band, back plate, nose, eight studs, a gold nose ball, cross plate, and brackets, pushing the overall total near 165 — comfortably within budget.

For positioning the studs, I'm calculating their locations around the boss front using trig, then building a helper function that places each arm part relative to the hub using a quaternion-based local offset and rotation.

Still writing orientation logic...

Verifying the quaternion rotation math checks out, then working out the cloth cell grid positions for the bays and columns across the lattice.

Adding the windboard slats with a backing rail, gold nail details along the spar front, and starting the tip cap sphere geometry.

Adding more hub details...

I'm figuring out how to type the Ctx parameter for buildCapAndRoof without conflicting with any existing module declaration, leaning toward an inline loose type annotation instead of redeclaring it.

Now I'm planning the cap and roof geometry: positioning the cap box and tower top dimensions, locating the hub and axle housing so sails mount cleanly at the front, and considering how to shape a rounded dome for the roof using a lathe profile, possibly scaling it to get a slightly elongated Dutch windmill cap shape.

Finial stem and ball bring the top to about 5.2. I'm adding a trim ring/drum beneath the roof—a short wood-colored cylinder at the eaves to mark the transition—before starting the dome lathe just above it.

For texture, I'm planning shingle rows as thin torus rings in a lighter roof color spaced along the dome's slope, plus small individual shingle boxes arranged in rings between them for added detail, keeping the total part count manageable by using about five rows of twelve boxes each, with radii computed from an interpolated profile function.

Sizing each shingle box to be wide tangentially, thin along the normal, and offset slightly outward so it sits embedded in the dome surface, alternating colors by row. Now I'm thinking about adding a small round gable window near the front above the hub/axle area.

I'll skip adding side windows and just do the front dormer, building its frame ring, glass disc, cross bars, and a small brow arc oriented using the surface normal so it leans correctly on the dome.

Now I'm checking whether the axle housing cylinder for the hub actually clears the dome surface at that height, since the computed dome radius there seems close to where the hub protrudes, so I need to verify the geometry doesn't clip through the shell.

Finishing the dome profile curve up to the top point at y=4.95, then adding a boxy wooden bonnet housing protruding at the front with a cylindrical boss, iron bands, and brass studs, with a hub boss extending to about z=1.02 that the sails' own hub cap will build on top of.

For the tail, I'm working out that the pole extends back from the cap toward tailPoleBack around (0, 4.1, -1.2), noting the box constraints mean it can't reach the ground, so the ladder will need to stop short rather than running all the way down.

I'm adding a horizontal handle bar at the pole's end with a small stake peg, then working out the exact coordinates so the pole emerges naturally from the back dome without clipping through it.

For the rods, I'm defining them using a helper that draws cylindrical connections with a given radius and side count, using fewer sides for a simpler pole look. Then I'm positioning a ladder beside the pole—figuring out where its rails should sit so they stay parallel to the pole and remain within the box bounds.

Adding a cross-bar handle and iron ring to the pole end, plus a finial on top of the dome with a small gold ball using the doorKnob color. Considering whether to add rib details or trim rings along the dome eaves, but shingles alone might be sufficient.

Now I'm working out the lathe collar that sits just under the roof base, defining its profile points and repositioning the roof's starting height so it sits properly above this new collar piece.

Adding a darkWood bonnet box on the dome front, a trimWood boss cylinder with gold studs, and an iron nose cap. Then I'm placing dentil blocks and a decorative torus ring around the collar's eave edge for added detail.

Now I'm working out the shingle rows - calculating radius-based counts per row to approximate realistic tapering, but noticing the part budget is tight at ~190 total pieces, so I'm trimming shingle width and counts down to keep things under budget, possibly merging shingles by color to save on parts.

I'll skip merging geometries and just rely on count reduction. For color, I'm alternating rows between roofLight and a complementary reddish tone rather than adding darker shading shingles, keeping the palette simple. I also need to skip shingle placement near the front where the bonnet/window sits, so I'm checking angular position against the window's height and azimuth to exclude overlapping shingles there.

Simplifying to just skip windows where z>0 and |x|<0.4, keeping row 0.1 since the bonnet doesn't start until rel 0.15, and only skipping rows from 0.24 upward. I'm alternating row angle offsets by index parity, then moving on to defining the dome's interpolation profile points.

Now I'm working out the lathe geometry itself — figuring that with 12 segments the dome's flat faces fall short of the ideal radius by a cosine factor, so I bump the segment count to 16 to tighten that error, and plan to offset the shingle boxes slightly outward from the surface so they sit mostly embedded with a small raised lip.

I'm also positioning the front window by interpolating the dome's radius profile at the relevant height, checking it lines up with the bonnet housing below, and computing the surface normal there so the window frame tilts to face up and forward rather than straight out.

Adding a sill box below the window, then topping off the piece with a finial: a slender rod, gold ball, and cone tip reaching up to around 5.2.

Now I'm defining a reusable `put` helper for placing parts with position, direction, and axis, then starting on the clock's bonnet housing—a boxy frame with darker trim bands for structure.

Adjusting the window and roof slab positions on the bonnet so they don't overlap: nudging the window higher to a relative y of 0.74 so its glass and frame clear the roof slab's lower edge.

For the dome rows, I'm figuring out which ring rows need their front shingles skipped to avoid clipping through the bonnet's window — row 0.66 has a large radius so skipping |x|<0.4 covers the front, and row 0.8 at radius 0.33 mostly overlaps the window's height range, so a general rule of skipping front-facing shingles when z>0 and |x|<0.4 should work across these rows. Now adding a small cylindrical boss detail near the bonnet position to represent a mounting piece.

For the bonnet, I'm placing a boss near the top, then adding small gold studs around its ring, a short iron nose cylinder extending forward, and dark iron bands wrapping the bonnet at specific heights to add detail. I'm also planning dentil boxes spaced around the eave just below the roof's starting height, making sure they sit beneath the collar without clipping the floor.

Skipping the dentil idea in favor of a ring of small scallop boxes along the roof's edge rim, then adding a row of dark wood collar studs facing outward near the collar line. I'm considering extra ridge ribs along the dome but deciding to skip them, and instead adding a small round vent detail on the back gable with a disc and slatted window frame pieces for texture.

Now I'm writing a reusable window helper function that computes position and normal direction from azimuth and height ratio, then using it to place a detailed front window and a simpler back vent, followed by a surface lookup function that finds which profile segment a given height falls into.

I'm also calculating shingle row placement: picking height levels, interpolating the radius at each, and dividing the circumference by shingle width to get how many shingles fit per row.

Computing the pole geometry with iron collar rings positioned along the rod's direction, then working out rail placement at matching heights and interpolated z-positions on either side.

Adding the small ring geometry and sorting out helper signatures for rods, boxes, and toruses with proper axis/direction handling.

I'm planning a buildTowerBody function using the provided Ctx type, designing a tapered octagonal tower shape with a lathe profile going from radius 1.55 to 1.05 across its height.

Actually, switching to CylinderGeometry with 8 segments is simpler -- rotating it so a flat face points forward (toward +Z) for the door placement, working out the apothem math to keep the geometry within the bounding box limits and aligned with the door surface at y=0.45.

Now I'm working through the radial taper for the tower walls, defining frustum layers for the cream wall, brick skirt base, and wood trim bands at bottom, mid, and top heights, coordinating these with the gallery deck position at y=2.

For the gallery, I'm figuring out the radius so it stays within the bounding box, sizing it as an octagon ring that protrudes slightly past the tower wall, positioned above the door. Then I'm placing eight posts at the octagon vertices with a connecting rail to form the gallery railing.

For the rounded cap at the top, I'm working out whether a torus would give the right octagonal silhouette, checking how its tubular segments align with the post angles so the facets line up correctly at the ring's circumference.

I'll stick with a cylinder segment for simplicity, rotating it 22.5° around Y so its flat faces align properly, and I'm sketching a helper function to build these octagonal pieces by specifying top/bottom radii, height range, and color.

For the corner ribs, I'm computing vertex positions at 45° intervals offset by 22.5° from +Z, then connecting bottom to top vertices with thin tapered rods pushed slightly outward from the radius to emphasize the edges, using a hexagonal cross-section for smoothness.

I'm also considering small brick-colored boxes placed on each face at various heights, accounting for the tower's taper angle (about 7.6° slope) so they sit flush against the sloped wall surface, oriented with the face normal direction.

Now I'm budgeting part count: wall, skirt, bands, ribs, deck, posts, rails, top ring, plus brick patches, keeping total near 170. I'm adding mortar-line rings on the skirt at a few heights and planning small brick tile clusters to texture the skirt surface.

Since individual brick boxes would blow the part budget, I'm switching to merging geometries per colour (brickDark and brickLight) into a single merged part each, composing each brick's transform matrix from position, rotation, and scale before merging.

I can use the SDK's aim helper to orient geometry toward a direction with a given up vector, and BufferGeometryUtils' mergeGeometries to combine indexed box geometries. I'm laying out the skirt bricks per face in rows, calculating face width at different heights using the polygon's apothem and tangent of the half-angle to size each brick row correctly.

Now I'm sizing bricks at roughly 0.36 wide with 3 per row, alternating offsets between rows, covering y from 0.6 to 1.05 with a slight protrusion, and merging all 72 bricks across 8 faces into two color-variant geometries (lighter and darker terracotta tones). I need to check how the door frame at the front face interacts with the skirt's protrusion so they don't visually clash where the door sits against the surface.

Since the door would poke through brick geometry on the front face, I decide to simply skip skirt bricks entirely on that face, and offset the skirt frustum slightly larger than the wall so it clears the door plane cleanly. Now I'm moving on to work out window placement.

Since exact window positions are unknown, I'll place small exposed-brick patches away from likely window spots—near the corner ribs at u≈±0.38, avoiding face centers where windows would sit. Each patch gets 3-5 jittered bricks for an irregular, weathered look, with roughly a dozen patches scattered around the tower.

I also want subtle plaster shading: a faint wallShade band low on the wall (around y 1.15-1.6) to suggest dirt or dampness near the base, plus trim bands—one near the bottom skirt (0.45-0.6) and another at the skirt top (1.05-1.17)—using trimWood with slight radius offsets.

For the remaining bands, I'll place a mid ring under the gallery deck as a darkWood corbel, and reconsider the mid trim position so it doesn't clip the windows, settling on roughly 1.05-1.17 for one and a top band around 3.6-3.78, keeping the bottom band fixed.

For the top cap, I'm working out the torus ring dimensions at y~3.82-3.91 to sit above the box, plus a flat darkWood disc underneath it and an octagonal wallShade plate near the top to finish the roof transition.

For the gallery deck at y 1.9-2.02, I'm sizing it as a darkWood octagon with radius 1.6, checking it clears the wall's circumference at that height, and planning corbel brackets beneath it to support the overhang.

Then I'm placing 8 posts at radius 1.52 running from y 2.02 to 2.55, using hexagonal rods with small cap spheres, plus top and mid rails connecting adjacent posts to form the railing.

Adding balusters between posts, merging all same-colored cylinders into single geometries using a helper that orients a cylinder between two points via quaternion rotation from the Y-axis. I'm keeping the front open near the door and building the octagonal top and mid rails as straight rod segments between post positions.

Now I'm attaching everything under the base bone, extending rod lengths slightly to cover corner gaps, and skipping extras like hooks or pennants. For the wall ribs, I'm placing vertical rods at each vertex running from near the base up through the gallery deck to the top, sized as a thin four-sided box-like section.

Rethinking the rib shape—since it sits at a vertex of an octagon, a four-sided section would look like a flat diamond rather than a rounded edge, so I'm switching to a rounded six-sided section instead for a smoother low-poly rib, tapering its radius slightly from bottom to top.

Now I'm placing the front door so it sits centered at a face, avoiding conflict with the rib vertices at ±22.5°. For the corbels under the deck, I'm positioning radial wedge-shaped boxes oriented along the Z-axis at each face center, spanning from the wall radius to the deck's larger apothem, and double-checking that the front corbel clears the space above the door.

I'm also adding a darker underside ring for the deck using a cylinder just below it, then switching to writing the helper functions: a radius function that tapers with height, an apothem calculation, and an octagonal frustum builder using cylinder geometry rotated 22.5° to align faces properly.

Now I'm working out the wall geometry spanning the full height, then calculating the face normal tilt angle by taking the derivative of the apothem slope so each wall panel can be oriented with the correct outward-facing direction.

For placing boxes onto these angled wall faces, I'm computing each box's center as a radial point along the surface plus a tangential offset for horizontal positioning and a small outward push along the normal for embedding depth, then composing the final transform matrix by aiming the box's local z-axis along that normal while keeping world-up as the reference.

I'm applying this transform to each box geometry, then grouping all shapes by color into buffer arrays so I can merge each color group into a single mesh at the end for efficiency.

Now I'm laying out skirt bricks per face, computing row heights and alternating column offsets with gaps so bricks tile the lower band without overhanging face edges, assigning colors with slight light/dark variation via a seeded RNG.

Checking face half-widths at the skirt's y-level confirm bricks fit within the frustum slope, then working out how far bricks protrude from the skirt surface and how the skirt itself grows slightly outward from the wall. Settling on a darker reddish-brown base color for the skirt to contrast with the bricks.

Choosing a small palette—brick dark, brick light, plank tone, and a cream highlight—then sketching out scattered brick patch positions across the upper wall faces by face index, height, and horizontal offset to break up the monotony.

I'm working out brick cluster geometry: two jittered rows of bricks protruding slightly from the wall surface, checking that patch spans don't collide with the vertical rib details near face edges, and nudging the horizontal placement so the brick groups sit clear of both the ribs and likely window positions.

Now I'm adding a thin mortar-colored backing slab beneath the bricks for a chipped-plaster effect, then moving on to the gallery deck -- a cylindrical platform set at a given height and thickness around the structure.

Still writing deck geometry...

I'm checking the apothem-to-vertex gap merges into one part, then verifying post positions at the vertex radius align with the deck's rotated octagon orientation, accounting for the 22.5° rotation offset.

For the railing structure, I'm placing darkWood posts with trimWood rails, adding spherical post caps, and computing baluster spacing based on the octagon's side length at radius 1.5, giving about 3 balusters per gap.

Tallying up the overall part count — wall, skirts, bands, shade, roof ring, deck layers, corbels, posts, rails, balusters, bricks — I'm landing around 35 parts, which stays comfortably under budget, so I'm considering adding a few more decorative touches like quoins or iron details for extra richness.

Positioning studs radially outward along each rib. I'm also adding a row of small dentil boxes in dark wood beneath the top band, spaced across each face, to give that trim some texture.

Now I'm working out the rib geometry for the tapered section, running endpoints along the cone's straight edges with a slight radial offset for thickness. For the top band's decorative ring, I'm using a torus rotated to lie flat around the octagonal frustum.

Rather than fight Euler order conventions to get the right combined rotation, I'm simplifying by baking the rotations directly into the geometry itself—rotating it about X then Y before placing the part—avoiding ambiguity from THREE's default 'XYZ' composition order. I'll apply the same approach to the cylinders for consistency.

Now I'm working through the torus vertex math—checking where tubular vertices land after the rotation, computing the apothem against the target radius, and solving for the torus's major/minor radius so the rim sits just outside the target value while staying under the overall size limit.

Writing merge and cylinder helpers...

Defining rail dimensions, then setting up a brick-face helper function that computes angled positions and surface offsets for the skirt panels using trig based on each face's angle and tilt.

I should also add a mid shade band octagon before the ribs for the wall shading, and include an optional name parameter on the wall part.
